purpose: Locate DDTree in using a trained language model, before introducing its specialized mechanism.
narration: Inference means using a trained model to produce an answer, rather than training it. For a typical language model, the prompt and generated text form a prefix used to predict the next token.
anchor: Inference uses the trained model. The prefix is the text available so far.

purpose: Make the repeated target-model calls the concrete bottleneck that motivates speculation.
narration: That is autoregressive decoding: choose a token, add it to the prefix, then run the target model again. Caching reuses earlier work, but the next-token decisions still form a sequential loop.
anchor: Cached earlier work; sequential next-token decisions. Not a measured timeline.

purpose: Introduce draft and target as distinct roles and explain why proposing a block can help.
narration: Speculative decoding adds a cheaper drafter. It proposes several tokens, then the target checks those positions together in one pass. Accepted proposals can advance several tokens while correct verification preserves the target's decoding behavior.
anchor: Cheap proposals plus correct target verification, not a replacement model.

purpose: Identify the remaining sequential work that motivates a parallel drafter.
narration: But a drafter that also predicts one token at a time still needs several dependent steps. Parallel checking does not make that drafting work parallel.
anchor: Focus on the drafter: one proposal can depend on the previous proposal.

purpose: Explain masked-token diffusion without implying that all diffusion generation uses one step.
narration: Masked-token diffusion offers another approach: learn to recover hidden text, updating several positions together. Many diffusion systems repeat that refinement; diffusion does not automatically mean one step.
anchor: Masked-token diffusion predicts hidden text, often through repeated refinement.

purpose: Place diffusion in the drafting stage and identify DFlash's single-pass, target-conditioned design.
narration: D Flash uses a small block-diffusion drafter to predict the whole block in one pass. It receives context features from the target's already-processed text. Diffusion accelerates the draft; the target remains autoregressive.
anchor: DFlash: one block-draft pass, conditioned on target context features.

purpose: Connect DFlash's alternative probabilities to DDTree's budget question, then motivate the worked example.
narration: A single drafted chain uses just one choice at each position. D D tree instead uses the alternative probabilities to build several possible paths under a verification budget. Which continuations deserve those slots?
anchor: DFlash supplies probabilities. DDTree allocates paths. The target verifies.

section: 1. Why buy more than one future?
purpose: Distinguish a cheap proposal from the model that actually decides.
narration: Now make that budget question concrete. We are completing a message: My dog stayed outside. Suppose the drafter proposes those last three words. Each word is one token in this tiny example.
anchor: A familiar message; one word per toy token.

section: 1. Why buy more than one future?
purpose: Make a missing branch a concrete lost opportunity, not an incorrect output.
narration: But the more expensive target model chooses cat, not dog. We write cat. The problem is wasted preparation: this chain continued the dog history, not the cat history.
anchor: A missing route stops reuse; it does not overrule the target.

section: 1. Why buy more than one future?
purpose: Motivate a fixed-budget choice between depth and alternatives.
narration: With the same three draft slots, we could prepare cat instead of the final word outside. Should we finish one possible sentence, or cover another beginning?
anchor: Same budget: a deeper chain or another branch?

purpose: Establish the factorized toy distribution and distinguish its role from the target.
narration: Here are the D Flash drafter's three position distributions: dog or cat, stayed or slept, then outside or inside. These probabilities are illustrative, not measured language statistics.
anchor: Toy word probabilities; every column sums to 1.

purpose: Explain why the surrogate reuses per-position probabilities across branches.
narration: Our draft model, Q, reuses these position probabilities on every path. The phrase dog stayed requires dog first, then stayed.
anchor: Q gives stayed the same probability after dog or cat.

purpose: Connect multiplication to the chance of reaching a complete prefix.
narration: Under this factorized model, multiply point six for dog by point seven for stayed: point four two. That is this prefix's chance under Q, not the target's confidence.
anchor: Prefix mass under Q: 0.60 x 0.70 = 0.420.

purpose: Establish the ancestor constraint needed for valid highest-mass selection.
narration: Extending to dog stayed outside multiplies by point eight. The mass falls to point three three six. Adding another requirement lowers the chance, so this descendant scores below its ancestors.
anchor: q(dog stayed outside) = 0.420 x 0.80 = 0.336.

purpose: Define matched length as one unit earned for each reached selected depth.
narration: Consider this candidate five-node tree. If the continuation is dog stayed outside, it earns three matches: dog, then stayed, then outside. One match for each selected depth.
anchor: Count one match per reached depth. The carried root is extra.

purpose: Show the first survival probability rather than merely displaying a sum.
narration: At depth one, both dog and cat are covered. Their chances add to one, so the first match is certain under our two-choice draft model.
anchor: Chance of at least 1 match: 0.600 + 0.400 = 1.000.

purpose: Make the second branch's contribution available before using it in the expectation.
narration: For cat stayed, use the same product rule: point four for cat, times point seven for stayed. That gives point two eight.

purpose: Connect mutually exclusive prefixes to the second survival probability.
narration: A second match needs dog stayed or cat stayed. Those are different possible messages. Their masses add to point seven, so we earn the second match seventy percent of the time under Q.
anchor: Chance of at least 2 matches: 0.420 + 0.280 = 0.700.

purpose: Connect the last selected depth to its contribution to matched length.
narration: Only dog stayed outside reaches a third selected depth. Its chance is point three three six.
anchor: Chance of at least 3 matches: 0.336.

purpose: Derive expectation by adding contributions, then connect it to the selection objective.
narration: Each reached depth contributes one match. Add those chances to get two point zero three six expected matches under Q. Equivalently, add the mass of every selected prefix.
anchor: Expected matches under Q = 1.000 + 0.700 + 0.336 = 2.036.

purpose: Derive the ranking rule from the objective and ancestor property.
narration: Each node costs one slot and contributes its prefix mass. Choose the largest masses. Because ancestors score higher than descendants, this selection also keeps the paths connected.
anchor: Fixed node budget + Q objective: take the highest prefix masses.

purpose: Model the first two selections before handing a choice to the viewer.
narration: Dog scores point six. Dog stayed scores point four two. Those are the first two prefixes to prepare.
anchor: Five draft slots. Prepared so far: dog, then dog stayed.

purpose: Ask the viewer to apply the score rule instead of following another narrated pop.
narration: Now choose. Should the next slot prepare cat, at point four, or finish dog stayed outside, at point three three six?
anchor: Your choice: cat at 0.400, or dog stayed outside at 0.336?

purpose: Explain the choice in terms of marginal contribution, not visual depth.
narration: Cat wins. Finishing the longer phrase is not automatically more valuable. Preparing cat contributes more expected matches under Q for the same one-slot cost.
anchor: Prepare cat: 0.400 > 0.336. Branching is not always better.

purpose: Complete the worked selection while compressing familiar comparisons.
narration: The next two choices are dog stayed outside and cat stayed. Five slots are full. Cat stayed outside is next in line, but outside the budget.
anchor: Five draft nodes selected. The carried word My is extra.

purpose: Test whether the viewer can transfer the ranking rule to concentrated probabilities.
narration: Now compare both distributions with three slots. Raise the chances of dog and stayed to point nine each. After dog and dog stayed, would you prepare cat or dog stayed outside?
anchor: Same three-slot budget on both sides. Predict: branch or depth?

purpose: Show that topology follows the distribution rather than a fixed preference for trees.
narration: Now dog stayed outside scores point six four eight, while cat scores only point one. The same rule chooses a chain. Cover another beginning only when its probability justifies the slot.
anchor: 0.90 x 0.90 x 0.80 = 0.648 > 0.100. Depth wins this time.

purpose: Distinguish allocation under Q from actual target-conditioned decisions.
narration: Return to our five-node tree. In this example, the target prefers outside after dog stayed, but inside after cat stayed. Both histories end in stayed, yet the earlier animal changes the prediction.
anchor: Same last word, different history: the target can predict differently.

purpose: Motivate flat storage and explicitly map prefix identity and language position.
narration: Pack the tree's words into one array. Stayed appears twice, once for each animal's history. Those entries share a language position, but are not interchangeable. Positions follow depth, not array order.
anchor: Six inputs: root + five draft nodes. Position = root position + depth.

purpose: Use the two meanings of stayed to make incorrect cross-branch attention concrete.
narration: Take stayed on the cat path. Each column is a token it might see. Should it be allowed to look at stayed on the dog path?
anchor: Can the cat's stayed see the dog's stayed?

purpose: Explain the mask as preserving conditional meaning rather than a matrix recipe.
narration: No. That would mix two different messages. On the cat path, stayed may see My, cat, itself, and earlier cached context. It must not borrow the dog's history.
anchor: Cat-path stayed sees My, cat, itself, and prior context.

purpose: Explain how one masked target pass supplies reusable, path-correct outputs.
narration: Apply that rule to every row. One target pass now produces a next-token distribution at each node, without leaking information between branches.
anchor: One target pass; separate path-conditioned outputs.

purpose: Make precomputed target outputs visible before traversal so reuse is not mistaken for another model call.
narration: For this toy run, suppose the choices from those target outputs are these. All these outputs are available before we walk a branch. Walking will read them, not recompute them.
anchor: Toy target choices, already available. Walking reads; it does not recompute.

section: 5. Follow the target, not the draft
purpose: Expose the misconception that the largest draft score chooses the output token.
narration: At My, the target chooses cat. The draft ranked dog higher. Which word goes into the message?
anchor: Draft prefers dog. Target chooses cat. What do we write?

section: 5. Follow the target, not the draft
purpose: Use an explicit conflicting decision to separate correctness from proposal ranking.
narration: Cat. The target decides. Because we prepared a cat branch, we can follow it and reuse the output already computed for that history.
anchor: Write cat; follow its prepared branch.

section: 5. Follow the target, not the draft
purpose: Demonstrate another matched step without implying a second target pass.
narration: After My cat, the target chooses stayed. We prepared that continuation too. Two speculative words have matched, without another target forward pass.
anchor: Write stayed; reuse its cat-path output. Two speculative matches.

section: 5. Follow the target, not the draft
purpose: Distinguish selecting an output token from processing it as a model input.
narration: Now the target chooses inside. We did not prepare that child. Write inside anyway, then stop this walk. The word has been selected, but not yet processed as a model input.
anchor: My cat stayed inside. Carry the unprocessed word inside into the next round.

section: 5. Follow the target, not the draft
purpose: Close the round with the correct state boundary and discard hypothetical histories.
narration: Keep the processed history My cat stayed in the target cache. Discard the unused dog history. Inside is the new bonus word: it becomes the next root and gets processed next round.
anchor: Cached: My cat stayed. The selected word inside is not cached yet.

section: 6. Change the draft, keep the target
purpose: Test the central model on two different trees with the same target decision.
narration: Return to the two three-slot trees. The target still wants My cat. Does a draft that strongly prefers the dog change the message, or only whether we prepared the useful route?
anchor: The target still wants My cat. Does changing the draft change the message?

section: 6. Change the draft, keep the target
purpose: Resolve the changed case and separate output identity from speculative reuse.
narration: Both write cat. The branched tree prepared that word and gets a speculative match. The dog-only chain did not, so cat becomes its next bonus immediately. Preparation changes; the target's decision does not.
anchor: Both write My cat. Preparing a route buys reuse, not authority.

section: 6. Change the draft, keep the target
purpose: Limit the surrogate optimality claim and consolidate the mechanism.
narration: D Flash makes drafting parallel. D D tree uses its scores to buy coverage. That ranking is optimal under Q and a fixed node budget, not necessarily for the target or for speed. Construction, verification, and cache work still cost time. The target still chooses the tokens.
anchor: Parallel drafting, budgeted coverage, unchanged target authority. Not free speedup.
